title: Elements of Primary Health Care
body:
## What it is
The "elements" are the eight basic services that primary health care (PHC) delivers at community level. Nursing review decks usually compress them into the word ELEMENTS. Each letter is a service area, and each has its own note in this set.

## Must-know facts
- E: Education for health (health teaching, prevention)
- L: Locally endemic disease control (diseases common in the area, plus the data used to track them)
- E: Expanded Program on Immunization
- M: Maternal and child health, including family planning
- E: Essential drugs (generic and herbal medicines)
- N: Nutrition
- T: Treatment of common diseases and injuries, including emergency services
- S: Sanitation and environmental health (safe water, toilets, waste, food safety)
- The Mental Health Program is taught in the same branch of most reviewers; see the last note in this set.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Assess the community first: which element is the biggest gap (for example low immunization coverage or unsafe water)? Assessing before acting is the nursing-process rule.
2. Prioritize problems that threaten life or spread quickly (outbreaks, unsafe water) before slower problems.
3. Deliver the service through the barangay health station or rural health unit, with the midwife, barangay health workers and community.
4. Teach and organize the community to sustain the service themselves. PHC stresses community participation, not nurse-only delivery.

## Key terms and steps
- Primary level of care: first contact, closest to home, lowest cost.
- Referral: the nurse sends clients to higher levels when the service is beyond the health center.

## How the exam asks about it
- "Which element does this activity belong to?" Example patterns: vaccine cold box = EPI; ORS demonstration = treatment or education; latrine construction = sanitation. Decide by the main purpose.
- A trap: teaching is part of every element, but "Education" is the element only when the activity itself is the health teaching.

## Memory aid
ELEMENTS (E-L-E-M-E-N-T-S) is the common reviewer mnemonic described above.

## Related topics
[[Primary Health Care]], [[Health Education and Competency-Based Teaching]], [[Locally Endemic Diseases]], [[Expanded Program on Immunization]], [[Maternal and Child Health]], [[Essential Drugs]], [[Nutrition]], [[Treatment of CD, NCD and Emergency Services]], [[Waste, Food Sanitation and Sanitation Laws]], [[Community Mental Health Program]]

## Check against your textbook
- Some books word the letters slightly differently (for example "Safe water and sanitation"). Verify the wording your school uses.

title: Health Education and Competency-Based Teaching
body:
## What it is
Health education is the first element of PHC. It helps people gain knowledge, change attitudes and practice healthy behavior. Competency-based teaching means teaching until the learner can actually perform the skill or behavior, not only recite facts.

## Must-know facts
- Three learning domains: cognitive (knowing), affective (feeling or valuing), psychomotor (doing).
- Competency-based teaching defines the exact behavior the learner must show at the end (for example, mixes ORS correctly), then teaches toward it and checks it by return demonstration.
- Teach-back is the strongest simple check of understanding: the learner explains it in their own words.
- Good teaching starts from the learner's readiness, culture, language and existing practices.
- Match the method to the domain: lecture for cognitive, demonstration for psychomotor, discussion or role play for affective.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Assess learning needs, literacy, beliefs and readiness first. Teaching someone who is not ready, or in a language they do not use, wastes effort.
2. Set measurable objectives (what the learner will be able to do).
3. Choose the method and aids that fit the objective and the group.
4. Teach in simple steps, from simple to complex and known to unknown.
5. Evaluate by observation, return demonstration or teach-back, then reinforce.

## Key terms and steps
- Return demonstration: learner performs the skill while the nurse watches.
- Community participation: people help plan and run teaching activities.
- Barangay health workers can be trained to multiply the nurse's teaching.

## Community and family teaching
Focus on a few key messages with demonstrations (handwashing, ORS preparation, breastfeeding position) in the local language, involving the mother and other decision makers in the family.

## How the exam asks about it
- "Which shows teaching was effective?" The answer is usually a behavior shown (return demonstration) rather than attendance or "the client said yes".
- Match the objective's verb to the domain. A verb like "demonstrate" points to psychomotor.

## Related topics
[[Three Levels of Prevention]], [[Elements of Primary Health Care]], [[Health Promotion]], [[Competency-Based Teaching]], [[Primary Health Care]]

## Check against your textbook
- Exact names of teaching models or frameworks your school uses (verify local policy).

title: Three Levels of Prevention
body:
## What it is
Prevention is organized by when it acts in the natural history of disease. Exam items give an activity and ask which level it belongs to.

## Must-know facts
- Primary prevention: before disease occurs. Health promotion (nutrition teaching, exercise) and specific protection (immunization, handwashing, safe water, helmet use).
- Secondary prevention: early detection and prompt treatment to stop progression (screening such as blood pressure checks, Pap smear, breast exam, case finding, prompt treatment of a diagnosed case).
- Tertiary prevention: after disease or disability is established. Limit disability and rehabilitate (physical therapy after stroke, teaching a client with diabetes to prevent foot complications).
- The same disease can have all three levels. Pick the level from the client's current stage, not from the disease name.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Identify where the client is: healthy and at risk, ill but undiagnosed, or diagnosed with complications.
2. Choose the activity that matches that stage.
3. Prefer higher up the chain (primary first) when the goal is community impact, because it is cheapest and prevents suffering.

## Key terms and steps
- Health promotion vs specific protection: both primary; promotion is general (nutrition education), protection is aimed at one disease (vaccine).
- Screening is secondary even when the person has no symptoms.

## How the exam asks about it
- "Identify the prevention": a short scenario of an activity; ask yourself, "Is the person already diagnosed? Is the aim to find disease early or to prevent it or to limit damage?"
- Trap: read the stem for what stage is described; the same vaccine-like or teaching activity can sit at different levels depending on the client's status.
- Trap: rehabilitation is tertiary, even though it feels like "treatment".

## Memory aid
Primary = Prevent, Secondary = Seek early, Tertiary = Take care of damage. This is my own invented aid.

## Related topics
[[Health Education and Competency-Based Teaching]], [[Epidemiology and FHSIS]], [[Expanded Program on Immunization]], [[Health Promotion]], [[Levels of Prevention]]

## Check against your textbook
- Some textbooks list health promotion and specific protection under primary; others label them separately. Verify how your school groups them.

title: Epidemiology and FHSIS
body:
## What it is
Epidemiology studies how often, where and why disease occurs in populations, then uses that knowledge to control it. The Field Health Services Information System (FHSIS) is the Philippine health-facility reporting system that gathers service and disease data from health centers upward to municipal, provincial and national levels.

## Must-know facts
- The epidemiologic triad: agent, host, environment. Control targets whichever link is easiest to break.
- Descriptive epidemiology looks at person, place and time. Analytic epidemiology tests why.
- Surveillance is continuous collection, analysis and use of data for action.
- Terms: endemic (usual constant presence), epidemic (clearly more than expected), pandemic (many countries), sporadic (scattered, occasional).
- FHSIS gathers data using tools at the health station such as target client lists or treatment records, a monthly report and a summary report. Reports are consolidated upward and used to plan.
- Data must be accurate, complete and timely to be useful.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Record every client contact accurately at the time of service; unrecorded care disappears from planning data.
2. Compile the monthly report on time and check it before sending.
3. Analyze trends locally (are cases rising? is coverage dropping?) and act.
4. Report notifiable diseases promptly through the surveillance system, because delays allow spread.
5. Feed results back to the community and barangay officials.

## Key terms and steps
- Outbreak investigation steps (general): verify the diagnosis, confirm the outbreak, define cases, find cases, describe by person-place-time, form a hypothesis, control, report.
- Notifiable disease: law requires reporting.

## How the exam asks about it
- Question stems describe a record or form and ask which FHSIS tool it is, or which statistic to compute from the data.
- Trap: epidemic vs endemic. Compare to the expected level, not to absolute numbers.

## Related topics
[[Vital Statistics]], [[Incidence, Prevalence and Population Pyramid]], [[Locally Endemic Diseases]], [[DOH]], [[Epidemiology and Endemic Diseases]]

## Check against your textbook
- Current FHSIS form names, reporting schedule and whether an electronic version replaced paper forms (verify local policy).

title: Locally Endemic Diseases
body:
## What it is
"Locally endemic" means a disease that is regularly present in an area. In the Philippines, reviewers commonly list diseases such as tuberculosis, dengue, malaria, schistosomiasis, filariasis, leprosy, rabies, soil-transmitted helminthiasis, diarrheal disease and others. Which ones are "endemic" depends on the province, so the nurse works from local data.

## Must-know facts
General control logic for each (concepts only; verify specifics locally):
- Tuberculosis: caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, airborne. Signs: cough of long duration, fever, night sweats, weight loss. Control: finding cases, directly observed treatment, BCG for infants, ventilation, cough etiquette.
- Dengue: virus spread by day-biting Aedes mosquitoes that breed in clean standing water. Signs: sudden high fever, headache, pain behind the eyes, rash, bleeding signs. Control: search and destroy breeding sites, cover and clean containers, protect from bites. Watch the critical phase when fever falls: shock risk.
- Malaria: protozoan spread by Anopheles mosquito (night-biting, breeds in clear running or slow water). Signs: cyclic fever with chills. Control: bed nets, prompt diagnosis and treatment, environmental control.
- Schistosomiasis: parasite whose cycle uses a freshwater snail; people are infected through skin contact with contaminated water. Control: treat cases, avoid wading, sanitary excreta disposal.
- Filariasis: worms spread by mosquitoes. Signs: swollen limbs. Control: mass drug treatment and vector control.
- Leprosy: slow bacterial disease, skin and nerve involvement, long contact needed to spread. Control: early multi-drug treatment and contact tracing.
- Rabies: viral, spread by saliva of an infected animal bite. Nearly always fatal once symptoms appear, so prevention matters.
- Soil-transmitted worms: spread through contaminated soil and poor sanitation; control by sanitation, footwear, handwashing and deworming.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Treat urgent signs first (severe dehydration, shock, severe bleeding, animal bite wound care).
2. Case finding and reporting to the rural health unit, because early reporting triggers community control.
3. Isolate or counsel as appropriate; follow the national treatment protocol.
4. Contact tracing and community clean-up or vector control.
5. Teach prevention and the importance of finishing treatment.

## Community and family teaching
Clean surroundings, remove standing water, cover water containers, use nets or repellents as advised, wash hands, wash a bite wound immediately and seek care.

## How the exam asks about it
- Matching disease to vector or reservoir (Aedes, Anopheles, snail, dog).
- Choosing the "most effective" control: breaking the transmission link (vector breeding, sanitation) beats treating each case alone.
- Trap: dengue's greatest danger is after the fever drops, not at the first fever.

## Related topics
[[Epidemiology and FHSIS]], [[Vital Statistics]], [[Expanded Program on Immunization]], [[Waste, Food Sanitation and Sanitation Laws]], [[Water Supply and Toilet Facilities]]

## Check against your textbook
- Treatment regimens, drug names, program names, and which diseases are formally "endemic" now (verify local policy).
- The outline does not list individual diseases under this heading; the list above comes from general knowledge.

title: Vital Statistics
body:
## What it is
Vital statistics are numbers on life events in a population: births, deaths, marriages. Nurses use them to describe community health and to compare places and years.

## Must-know facts
- A rate has a numerator (events), a denominator (the population at risk) and a multiplier (per 1,000, per 100,000, per 100).
- Crude birth rate: live births divided by midyear population, times 1,000.
- Crude death rate: deaths divided by midyear population, times 1,000.
- Infant mortality rate: infant deaths (under one year) divided by live births, times 1,000.
- Maternal mortality ratio: maternal deaths divided by live births, times 100,000 (a ratio, since the denominator is live births, not women).
- Neonatal mortality: deaths in the first 28 days per 1,000 live births.
- Fetal death ratio, case fatality rate and proportionate mortality use different denominators; read the denominator carefully.
- Sex ratio: number of males divided by number of females, times 100.
- Swaroop's index: deaths of persons 50 years or older divided by total deaths, times 100. A higher value suggests better health conditions, because more people reach old age.
- Midyear population is used because the population changes during the year.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Pick the correct formula from what the question asks (births, deaths, infants?).
2. Check the denominator and the multiplier before computing.
3. Interpret: compare with earlier years or other areas, not just a single number.
4. Use trends to set priorities with the barangay and rural health unit.

## Key terms and steps
- Vital statistics sources: civil registration records, health facility reports and surveys.
- Natality = births, mortality = deaths, morbidity = illness.

## How the exam asks about it
- Computation stems: identify the denominator first. Trap: using total population when the formula needs live births.
- Trap: Swaroop's index counts deaths of those 50 and above in the numerator, not the population.

## Memory aid
For Swaroop: "Old deaths over all deaths." This is my own phrase.

## Related topics
[[Incidence, Prevalence and Population Pyramid]], [[Epidemiology and FHSIS]], [[Maternal and Child Health]]

## Check against your textbook
- Exact multipliers and definitions (some texts differ on neonatal or fetal ratios) (verify local policy).

title: Incidence, Prevalence and Population Pyramid
body:
## What it is
Incidence and prevalence measure illness in a population. A population pyramid is a graph of age and sex groups that shows the shape of the population.

## Must-know facts
- Incidence: NEW cases in a period among the population at risk. It measures risk of getting the disease.
- Prevalence: ALL existing cases (old plus new) at a point or over a period. It measures how widespread a disease is.
- Prevalence rises when new cases rise, or when people live long with the disease (chronic illness, improving treatment); it falls with cure or death.
- Incidence uses people who could still get the disease as the denominator; prevalence uses the whole population.
- Population pyramid: age groups on the vertical axis, males on one side and females on the other.
- A wide base and narrow top (an expanding pyramid) suggests high birth rate and many young dependents. A narrow base means falling births (aging population). A roughly rectangular shape means stable low birth and death.
- Dependency ratio: people too young or too old to work compared with working-age people.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Decide whether the question asks about new cases (incidence) or all cases (prevalence).
2. Read the pyramid shape to plan services: many children means immunization and nutrition programs; many elderly means noncommunicable disease and geriatric services.

## Key terms and steps
- Attack rate: incidence during an outbreak among those exposed.
- Point prevalence is at one moment; period prevalence is over time.

## How the exam asks about it
- "Which rate tells how many people newly developed...?" The answer is incidence.
- Trap: a better treatment that keeps people alive raises prevalence without raising incidence.
- Interpret what a base-heavy pyramid implies for the community nurse's priorities.

## Memory aid
Incidence = "Incoming" new cases; Prevalence = "Pool" of all cases. This is my own aid.

## Related topics
[[Vital Statistics]], [[Epidemiology and FHSIS]], [[Health Promotion]]

## Check against your textbook
- Wording of your school's formulas and pyramid types (verify local policy).

title: Expanded Program on Immunization
body:
## What it is
The Expanded Program on Immunization (EPI) is the national program that protects children (and pregnant women) against vaccine-preventable diseases through routine and catch-up vaccination. Its goal is high coverage so that the whole community is protected.

## Must-know facts
- Herd (community) immunity: when enough people are immune, the disease cannot spread easily, which also protects those who cannot be vaccinated.
- Routine immunization is delivered on scheduled days at health facilities, usually with outreach to remote areas.
- Chikiting Ligtas is the Philippine name for mass or catch-up immunization campaigns (for example measles and polio rounds) that supplement routine service. It reaches children missed by routine visits. Dates and details: verify local policy.
- A national law on mandatory immunization of infants and children exists (RA 10152, Mandatory Infants and Children Health Immunization Act, as commonly taught). Verify what it requires.
- Target setting: the number of eligible children is estimated from the population (using a percentage of the total population for infants, as stated in your textbook), then divided across the months or sessions to plan vaccines and supplies. Use your textbook's percentages; they are not given here.
- A child is counted as "fully immunized" when all the vaccines listed in the national definition are completed within the age limit. Verify the current definition.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Check each child's immunization card and screen for contraindications before vaccinating. Safety comes first.
2. Give the vaccine correctly (right vaccine, route, site, dose, interval).
3. Record in the child's card and the register.
4. Teach the caregiver what to expect and when to return.
5. Track defaulters and follow up at home.
6. Plan supplies from the target population, with a buffer for wastage and a working cold chain.

## Key terms and steps
- Defaulter: child who missed a scheduled dose; follow up and give the missed dose without restarting the series.
- Coverage: vaccinated divided by target, times 100.
- Dropout rate: those who got the first dose but not the later ones.

## Community and family teaching
Keep the vaccination card; return on the scheduled date; mild fever or soreness is common; bring the child even if mildly ill with a cold (mild illness alone is usually not a reason to postpone), but report severe reactions.

## How the exam asks about it
- Questions on the elements of the program, definitions, coverage computation and which activity addresses a low-coverage barangay.
- Trap: a vaccine missed does not require restarting the series; resume where it left off.

## Related topics
[[Cold Chain and Vaccine Logistics]], [[Vaccine Principles and Nursing Responsibilities]], [[BCG and Pentavalent Vaccine]], [[Tetanus Toxoid Immunization]], [[Epidemiology and FHSIS]]

## Check against your textbook
- The current schedule, the list of vaccines in the program, the fully immunized child definition and target percentages (verify local policy).

title: Cold Chain and Vaccine Logistics
body:
## What it is
The cold chain is the system that keeps vaccines at the correct temperature from manufacturer to the child. A broken cold chain makes vaccines lose potency without any visible change.

## Must-know facts
- Vaccines are sensitive to heat, and some (for example ones containing an adjuvant) are damaged by freezing.
- Typical principle: most vaccines are stored in a refrigerator at about 2 to 8 degrees Celsius; some freeze-dried vaccines can be frozen at the supply level. Check your textbook for which vaccines are kept in which compartment.
- Equipment at the health center level: a vaccine refrigerator (or ice-lined unit), a thermometer, cold boxes and vaccine carriers with frozen ice packs for outreach.
- The temperature is checked and recorded at least twice a day, including on weekends where required, to catch a failure early.
- Protect vaccines from direct light, especially some that are light-sensitive.
- Vaccine vial monitors, shake test and expiry date are used to judge vaccine quality.
- "First expiry, first out" stock management: use the vials that expire first.
- Open-vial rules depend on the vaccine; reconstituted vaccines have a short use time and must be discarded after the session.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Keep the cold chain unbroken: the first action on finding a temperature problem is to protect the vaccines (move them to a working cold box) and report, before deciding about use.
2. Check and record temperatures routinely.
3. Do not store food, drinks or other items in the vaccine refrigerator.
4. Arrange vials so air can circulate; place the most freeze-sensitive vaccines away from the cooling element.
5. Do not use a vaccine that has been exposed to heat or freezing until the supervisor decides it is safe.
6. Take inventory and request supplies on a schedule to avoid stock-outs.

## Key terms and steps
- Logistics management: forecast, order, receive, store, distribute, and monitor supplies.
- Wastage: unused doses discarded; multi-dose vials affect planning.

## How the exam asks about it
- "Where in the refrigerator?" or "What to do when power fails?" Think: protect the vaccine first.
- Trap: freezing damages some vaccines even though they look normal; cold is not always safe.

## Memory aid
"Cold, dark, not frozen (except some), and first-to-expire out." This is my own summary.

## Related topics
[[Expanded Program on Immunization]], [[Vaccine Principles and Nursing Responsibilities]]

## Check against your textbook
- The exact temperature ranges, shelf placement per vaccine, how long vaccines last in a carrier and the open-vial policy (verify local policy).

title: Vaccine Principles and Nursing Responsibilities
body:
## What it is
General rules that apply to every vaccine, plus a quick comparison of the main childhood vaccines. This is the "table" idea: for each vaccine know its type (live or inactivated), route, site, and key precaution.

## Must-know facts
- Live attenuated vaccines (examples: BCG, measles-containing vaccines, oral polio, rotavirus) use weakened organisms. They are generally avoided in people who are severely immunocompromised and in pregnancy.
- Inactivated or toxoid vaccines (examples: tetanus toxoid, pertussis and diphtheria components, hepatitis B, inactivated polio) cannot cause the disease.
- Route and site matter: intradermal, subcutaneous, intramuscular or oral. Giving the wrong route reduces effect or increases reaction. Infants usually receive intramuscular injections in the front-outer thigh.
- Contraindication principle: a severe allergic reaction to a previous dose or to a component is a true reason not to give that vaccine again. Mild illness, low-grade fever, cough, mild diarrhea or malnutrition are usually NOT reasons to delay (verify local policy).
- Common mild reactions: soreness, redness, low fever, irritability. Severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is rare but needs emergency action.
- Several vaccines can be given on the same day at separate sites with separate syringes.
- Never mix vaccines in one syringe unless the manufacturer says so.
- Use a new sterile syringe and needle for each child; follow safe disposal in a sharps container.
- Missed doses: continue the series; do not restart.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Screen: ask about prior severe reactions, current illness, and special conditions. Safety before giving.
2. Check the vaccine (name, expiry, appearance, vaccine vial monitor) and prepare it correctly.
3. Explain to the caregiver and obtain consent.
4. Give with correct technique, route and site; keep epinephrine and emergency supplies available.
5. Observe the child for a short time afterwards for immediate reactions.
6. Document and teach about expected effects and when to seek help.
7. Report serious adverse events following immunization to the proper office.

## Key terms and steps
- Adverse event following immunization (AEFI): any untoward medical event after a vaccine, whether or not caused by it.
- Anaphylaxis: airway swelling, breathing difficulty, drop in blood pressure; first action is call for help and give emergency treatment per protocol.

## How the exam asks about it
- "Which child should NOT be vaccinated today?" Look for a history of a severe reaction to the same vaccine, not for a runny nose.
- "Which vaccine is live?" Know the list.
- Trap: pregnancy and live vaccines.

## Related topics
[[Expanded Program on Immunization]], [[Cold Chain and Vaccine Logistics]], [[BCG and Pentavalent Vaccine]], [[Tetanus Toxoid Immunization]]

## Check against your textbook
- Which vaccines are in the current Philippine schedule (for example rotavirus, pneumococcal, HPV, measles-rubella variations), their ages, doses, and sites (verify local policy). I have not listed doses or ages here.

title: BCG and Pentavalent Vaccine
body:
## What it is
BCG protects against severe forms of tuberculosis in young children. The pentavalent vaccine combines protection against five diseases in one injection: diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, hepatitis B and Haemophilus influenzae type b.

## Must-know facts
- BCG is a live vaccine given into the skin (intradermal). It is given early in life, often at birth (verify the policy for timing and age limits).
- Expected BCG reaction: a small papule after a few weeks, which may become a pustule, ulcerate and heal with a scar over a few months. This is normal and does not need dressings or ointment.
- BCG is generally avoided in severe immunocompromise (for example symptomatic HIV) and in children with generalized skin disease (verify local policy).
- BCG gives partial protection: it helps prevent severe childhood TB like meningitis, not all adult lung TB.
- Pentavalent: DPT plus hepatitis B plus Hib. It is given intramuscularly in the front-outer thigh of the infant, in a series of three doses spaced about a month apart or similar (verify the exact ages and intervals).
- Mild reactions: fever, local pain and swelling, irritability. A fever-reducing measure may be advised per local policy.
- Severe reactions to a previous dose (high continuous crying, convulsions, collapse, encephalopathy) are reasons to withhold further pertussis-containing doses (verify local policy).

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Screen for contraindications and previous reactions.
2. Prepare and give the vaccine with the correct route: BCG intradermal (a wheal forms), pentavalent intramuscular.
3. Do not massage the BCG site or cover with unneeded dressing; for pentavalent, apply light pressure only if needed.
4. Teach expected reactions and warning signs (spreading redness, high fever, convulsion).
5. Record and schedule the next dose.

## Key terms and steps
- A wheal at the BCG site means the injection went into the skin layer.
- If a deep, painful abscess or enlarged nearby lymph node develops, refer.

## How the exam asks about it
- Route and site questions; normal BCG reaction vs a complication.
- "Which diseases does pentavalent protect against?" Name all five.
- Trap: a small ulcer and scar after BCG is expected, not an infection requiring antibiotics.

## Memory aid
Pentavalent = penta = five diseases (D, P, T, HepB, Hib). Standard idea, not my invention.

## Related topics
[[Vaccine Principles and Nursing Responsibilities]], [[Expanded Program on Immunization]], [[Locally Endemic Diseases]]

## Check against your textbook
- Dose volumes, exact ages and intervals, site (arm side for BCG), and which pentavalent product the program currently uses (verify local policy).

title: Maternal and Child Health
body:
## What it is
The Maternal and Child Health (MCH) program aims to reduce illness and death in mothers, newborns and children through care before, during and after pregnancy, and through child health services at community level.

## Must-know facts
- Prenatal care in the community: registration early in pregnancy, regular visits, weight and blood pressure checks, urine tests, abdominal exam, iron and folic acid supplements, tetanus protection, and teaching on diet, rest and danger signs. The number and timing of visits differ by source (verify local policy).
- Danger signs in pregnancy that need immediate referral: vaginal bleeding, severe headache with blurred vision, convulsions, swelling of face and hands, severe abdominal pain, fever, decreased fetal movement, leaking fluid.
- Birth planning: skilled attendant, health facility delivery, transport and emergency fund arrangements, and a blood donor if needed.
- Postpartum care: early visits, check bleeding, uterus, temperature, wound healing, breastfeeding, mood, and family planning counseling.
- Breastfeeding: exclusive for the first six months, started within the first hour, on demand, with proper attachment; continue with complementary foods after six months. Mother-baby friendly practices (rooming-in, no pacifiers or bottles) support it. Verify the law and policy details.
- Child health: growth monitoring (weight and length), immunization, vitamin A, deworming, ORS for diarrhea, and care for pneumonia and fever.
- IMCI (Integrated Management of Childhood Illness): a systematic approach, assess, classify, then treat, using color-coded categories (urgent referral, treatment and advice, or home care). General danger signs in a sick child: unable to drink or breastfeed, vomits everything, convulsions, lethargy or unconscious.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Identify danger signs first; refer urgently before routine tasks.
2. Assess the mother or child fully (history, vital signs, growth).
3. Treat or give supplements per protocol.
4. Teach the caregiver the key actions at home.
5. Follow up and record.

## Key terms and steps
- Risk approach: identify high-risk mothers (very young, older, many births, short spacing, prior complications) for more frequent care.
- Safe motherhood: pregnancy, delivery and postpartum care that is safe.

## Community and family teaching
Eat varied foods, take iron-folic acid, deliver with a skilled attendant, breastfeed exclusively, complete the child's vaccines, use ORS and continue feeding in diarrhea, return at once for danger signs.

## How the exam asks about it
- Which finding needs immediate referral or action? Pick the life-threatening danger sign.
- IMCI questions: first decide if a general danger sign is present; if yes, urgent referral follows.

## Related topics
[[Reproductive Health and Family Planning]], [[Tetanus Toxoid Immunization]], [[EINC and Active Management of Third Stage of Labor]], [[BEmOC and CEmOC]], [[Newborn Screening]], [[Expanded Program on Immunization]], [[Nutrition]]

## Check against your textbook
- The minimum prenatal visit schedule, the exact IMCI color categories and treatment plans, and the details of the breastfeeding law (verify local policy).

title: Reproductive Health and Family Planning
body:
## What it is
Reproductive health is complete physical, mental and social well-being in all matters of the reproductive system. In the Philippines, services are guided by a national Responsible Parenthood and Reproductive Health law (commonly cited as RA 10354; verify its details).

## Must-know facts
- Family planning lets couples decide the number and spacing of children. Counseling must be voluntary and informed, respecting the couple's choice and religion.
- Natural family planning methods: calendar (rhythm), basal body temperature, cervical mucus (ovulation) method, symptothermal, standard days method, lactational amenorrhea method (LAM).
- LAM works when the baby is under six months, the mother is exclusively breastfeeding and her menses have not returned. If one condition fails, advise another method.
- Barrier methods: condom (also protects against sexually transmitted infections), diaphragm.
- Hormonal methods: pills, injectables, implants. Teach use, common side effects (spotting, nausea) and warning signs.
- Intrauterine device: inserted by trained provider; teach the string check and danger signs.
- Permanent methods: voluntary tubal ligation and vasectomy, which require informed consent.
- Reproductive health elements often listed: maternal and child health, family planning, prevention of abortion complications, adolescent health, sexually transmitted infections and HIV, reproductive tract cancers, violence against women, male reproductive health and elderly care.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Assess the client's needs, history, medical conditions and wishes before suggesting a method.
2. Give complete information on options, effectiveness and side effects.
3. Let the client choose; support their decision.
4. Teach correct use and warning signs.
5. Provide follow-up and referral for conditions that prohibit a method.

## Key terms and steps
- Effectiveness: perfect use vs typical use.
- Dual protection: a condom with another method.

## Community and family teaching
Involve both partners, correct myths, and tell them where to get services and what to do for missed pills or problems.

## How the exam asks about it
- Which method fits a described client (breastfeeding, smoker, wants natural method)?
- Trap: do not pick a method for the client; counseling respects choice.
- Know the signs for which a client should return (for example IUD string missing, severe abdominal pain).

## Related topics
[[Maternal and Child Health]], [[VAWC and Violence Against Women and Children]], [[Health Promotion]]

## Check against your textbook
- Which methods the DOH currently provides and their rules (verify local policy). Pill and injectable names, doses and schedules are not given here.

title: Tetanus Toxoid Immunization
body:
## What it is
Tetanus toxoid (TT) is given to women of childbearing age, especially during pregnancy, to protect the mother and the newborn from tetanus. Neonatal tetanus is caused by bacterial spores entering the umbilical stump, usually after unclean cord care.

## Must-know facts
- The toxoid is inactivated, so it is safe in pregnancy.
- Protection builds with repeated doses spaced over weeks to years. Textbooks list a series of up to five doses, with each dose giving longer protection (verify the intervals and percentages in your textbook).
- Antibodies cross the placenta, so a mother who is protected passes protection to the baby (passive immunity).
- It is given intramuscularly, usually in the upper arm.
- Clean delivery and cord care are also essential: clean hands, clean cutting instrument, clean cord tie, and no harmful substances on the cord.
- Neonatal tetanus signs usually begin after the first few days: baby stops sucking, stiffness and spasms, fever may be present.
- Some programs have moved from TT to a combined tetanus and diphtheria vaccine; verify local policy.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Check the woman's immunization status and card first. This decides which dose she needs.
2. Screen for contraindications (severe reaction to a previous dose).
3. Give the dose correctly and record on the TT card and the maternal record.
4. Teach side effects (arm soreness, mild fever) and the next visit.
5. Teach clean cord care and clean delivery.

## Key terms and steps
- A woman fully protected earlier may need fewer new doses; check the card.
- Assess a new pregnancy against the prior doses given.

## How the exam asks about it
- Questions pair "which dose number" with the interval or protection given.
- Trap: do not restart the series if a dose was late.

## Related topics
[[Maternal and Child Health]], [[Expanded Program on Immunization]], [[Vaccine Principles and Nursing Responsibilities]], [[EINC and Active Management of Third Stage of Labor]]

## Check against your textbook
- The dose intervals, the percentage of protection at each dose, and whether Td replaces TT locally (verify local policy).

title: EINC and Active Management of Third Stage of Labor
body:
## What it is
EINC (Essential Intrapartum and Newborn Care) is a set of evidence-based practices for the time of birth and the first hours of the newborn. AMTSL (Active Management of the Third Stage of Labor) is a set of steps to deliver the placenta safely and prevent postpartum hemorrhage.

## Must-know facts
EINC core practices, in order for a well newborn (concept; verify details in current DOH materials):
- Immediate and thorough drying right after birth; this also stimulates breathing. Do not wipe off the white coating (vernix) as part of routine.
- Skin-to-skin contact of the baby with the mother's chest.
- Properly timed cord clamping, not immediately, after the cord stops pulsating or after a short delay.
- Non-separation of mother and baby for early and exclusive breastfeeding, with the first breastfeed within the first hour.
- Then routine newborn care such as eye care, vitamin K, and vaccines per policy, delayed until after the skin-to-skin period.
- Bathing is delayed for some hours.

AMTSL typical components:
- A uterotonic (oxytocin is the usual one) given soon after the baby is born, after checking that there is no second baby.
- Controlled cord traction with counter-pressure on the uterus above the pubic bone.
- Uterine massage after the placenta comes out, then teach the mother to check her own uterus.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. If the newborn is not breathing or crying, stop routine steps and start resuscitation. Airway and breathing come first (ABC).
2. For a well baby, do the EINC sequence in order, because the order protects warmth, bonding and breastfeeding.
3. Do AMTSL steps in the correct order; check the placenta is complete and uterus is firm.
4. Monitor bleeding, uterine firmness and vital signs for the first hours.
5. Record and teach the mother about breastfeeding and cord care.

## Key terms and steps
- Fundus firm and at or below the umbilicus is the goal; a soft uterus is massaged and bleeding is reported.
- Retained placenta or heavy bleeding is an emergency and calls for referral.

## How the exam asks about it
- Sequence questions: which comes first after birth? (drying and skin-to-skin come before routine injections and weighing).
- AMTSL: oxytocin first, then controlled traction, then massage.
- Trap: skipping drying or separating a well baby for routine procedures goes against EINC.

## Memory aid
Dry, skin, clamp late, feed. This is my own short summary.

## Related topics
[[BEmOC and CEmOC]], [[Newborn Screening]], [[Maternal and Child Health]], [[Expanded Program on Immunization]]

## Check against your textbook
- Timing of cord clamping, timing of vitamin K and vaccine, and dose or route of oxytocin (not stated here) (verify local policy).
outlineRefs: Active Management of Third Stage of Labor

title: BEmOC and CEmOC
body:
## What it is
Emergency obstetric and newborn care is organized into two levels. BEmOC (Basic Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care) covers life-saving services that a well-equipped health center can provide. CEmOC (Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care) includes everything in BEmOC plus surgery and blood transfusion at a hospital.

## Must-know facts
BEmOC signal functions (general list; verify the current version):
- Give parenteral antibiotics
- Give a parenteral uterotonic (oxytocin) drug
- Give a parenteral anticonvulsant (magnesium sulfate) for pre-eclampsia or eclampsia
- Manual removal of the placenta
- Removal of retained products of conception
- Assisted vaginal delivery (vacuum or forceps)
- Basic newborn resuscitation

CEmOC adds:
- Cesarean section
- Blood transfusion

- A BEmOC facility needs trained staff available around the clock and a referral link to a CEmOC facility.
- Common causes of maternal death worldwide: hemorrhage, hypertensive disorders, sepsis, obstructed labor, unsafe abortion. These explain the signal functions.
- Delays that kill: delay in deciding to seek care, delay reaching the facility, delay in receiving care at the facility.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Recognize the emergency early (heavy bleeding, convulsions, fever, prolonged labor).
2. Start stabilizing measures within scope: call for help, position, IV access, oxygen, give the ordered or protocol-based drug.
3. Refer with a clear message, and send the client with a trained escort if possible.
4. Communicate with the receiving facility so they prepare.
5. Document and follow up.

## Key terms and steps
- Network of facilities: the barangay health station, rural health unit, BEmOC facility and CEmOC hospital form a referral chain.

## How the exam asks about it
- "Which service belongs to CEmOC but not BEmOC?" The answer is surgery and blood transfusion.
- Trap: magnesium sulfate for seizures belongs to basic care.

## Memory aid
CEmOC = BEmOC + Cut (cesarean) + Blood. This is my own aid.

## Related topics
[[EINC and Active Management of Third Stage of Labor]], [[Maternal and Child Health]], [[DOH]]

## Check against your textbook
- Current signal function list and the standards for facilities (verify local policy).

title: Newborn Screening
body:
## What it is
Newborn screening (NBS) is a blood test done on the newborn to detect certain treatable inherited metabolic and endocrine disorders before symptoms appear, so treatment can prevent disability or death. In the Philippines it is backed by the Newborn Screening Act (commonly cited as RA 9288; verify).

## Must-know facts
- A few drops of blood from a heel prick are collected on special filter paper and dried.
- Timing: usually taken after the baby has fed for some time and is about one day old or more (commonly 24 to 48 hours). Testing too early can miss disorders. Verify the exact window; special rules apply to babies who are preterm or sick.
- Core disorders usually listed: congenital hypothyroidism, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, galactosemia, phenylketonuria, and G6PD deficiency. The program has expanded the panel; verify the current list.
- Screening is NOT a diagnosis. A positive screen needs a confirmatory test and prompt treatment.
- Untreated, these disorders may cause intellectual disability, growth problems or death.
- Parents have a right to be informed; refusal requires documentation per policy.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Explain the test to parents and get consent/documentation.
2. Collect the sample at the correct time using the correct site (the side of the heel), after warming the foot.
3. Fill in the card completely and let the blood dry without heat or contact.
4. Send the sample to the screening center promptly.
5. Trace babies with positive or unclear results quickly, because early treatment matters.
6. Teach parents to follow up for results.

## Key terms and steps
- Why the heel: it is easy to reach with minimal harm if the correct lateral area is used.
- Do not squeeze the heel repeatedly; do not layer blood or smear.

## Community and family teaching
Explain that a normal-looking baby can still have a disorder, that the test is important even if there is no family history, and that parents should ask for the result.

## How the exam asks about it
- Timing, specimen handling errors and the meaning of a positive screen.
- Trap: a positive screen is not a diagnosis. Collecting too early can miss disorders, and collecting too late delays treatment, so use the correct window.

## Related topics
[[EINC and Active Management of Third Stage of Labor]], [[Maternal and Child Health]], [[Expanded Program on Immunization]]

## Check against your textbook
- The exact window, the number of disorders in the current panel and what happens to babies born at home (verify local policy).

title: VAWC and Violence Against Women and Children
body:
## What it is
VAWC means Violence Against Women and their Children. The Philippine law is commonly cited as RA 9262, the Anti-Violence Against Women and Their Children Act of 2004 (verify). It covers abuse by a husband, former partner or someone with whom the woman has or had a sexual or dating relationship.

## Must-know facts
- Forms of abuse: physical, sexual, psychological/emotional, and economic.
- Protection orders can be sought, including a barangay protection order from the barangay and orders from the court. Violation can be punished. Verify the details.
- Health workers have roles in screening, treatment, documentation and referral.
- Abuse can affect children directly or through witnessing. A separate child-protection law exists (commonly cited as RA 7610; verify).
- Warning signs: unexplained or repeated injuries, injuries in different stages of healing, fearful behavior, delay in seeking care, inconsistent story.
- The cycle of violence is often described: tension building, acute violence, then a reconciliation or "honeymoon" phase.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Treat injuries and ensure immediate safety first. Life and safety come before the legal process.
2. Provide a private, calm, nonjudgmental setting. Believe the client; do not blame.
3. Document objectively using the client's own words and body maps.
4. Preserve evidence if the client agrees and per protocol.
5. Refer to the Women and Children Protection Unit/desk, social worker, police and legal help.
6. Safety plan: where to go, who to call, important documents.
7. Respect confidentiality and the client's pace of decision.

## Community and family teaching
Abuse is not the victim's fault, help is available, keep emergency numbers and a safety plan, and know where the nearest protection office is.

## How the exam asks about it
- First action with a suspected abuse victim: ensure safety and treat injuries; not confronting the abuser.
- Trap: do not pressure the client to leave or press charges immediately.

## Related topics
[[Reproductive Health and Family Planning]], [[Maternal and Child Health]], [[Community Mental Health Program]]

## Check against your textbook
- Exact law provisions, the sequence of protection orders and mandatory reporting rules for health workers (verify local policy).

title: Essential Drugs
body:
## What it is
Essential drugs are medicines that satisfy the priority health needs of most people and should be available at a price the community can afford. Philippine PHC also promotes generic medicines and tested herbal medicines as lower-cost options.

## Must-know facts
- Generic medicines use the chemical (generic) name and are cheaper than brands with the same active ingredient. A Generics Act exists (commonly cited as RA 6675; verify).
- The Traditional and Alternative Medicine Act (commonly cited as RA 8423; verify) supports research and use of traditional medicine.
- DOH endorses a set of herbal plants as evidence-based. The list reviewers commonly give is ten plants with their main use (verify each with your textbook):
  - Lagundi: cough and mild asthma
  - Sambong: diuretic, helps with kidney stones
  - Tsaang gubat: stomach pain and diarrhea
  - Akapulko: fungal skin infections (tinea, ringworm)
  - Niyog-niyogan: intestinal worms (do not chew excess)
  - Bawang (garlic): may lower cholesterol
  - Bayabas (guava): wound wash, mouth gargle for toothache
  - Yerba buena: pain relief
  - Ulasimang bato (pansit-pansitan): may lower uric acid (gout)
  - Ampalaya: may lower blood sugar
- Herbal medicines complement but do not replace proven treatment for serious illness.
- Barangay health stations may keep a small stock of essential medicines (sometimes called a barangay drug store); verify local policy.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Assess the client's condition, allergies, current drugs and use of herbs. Safety checks come first.
2. Refer serious or unresponsive illness; do not delay needed treatment for herbal remedies.
3. Teach correct preparation, dose and duration of the herbal remedy using verified sources.
4. Teach that herbs can interact with prescribed drugs.
5. Promote generic names and rational drug use (right drug, right dose, right time, completing courses).

## Key terms and steps
- Rational drug use: using medicine only when needed, correctly.
- Decoction: boiling plant parts; the standard preparation for many leaves.

## Memory aid
Pair each plant with one organ system or symptom (cough, kidney, skin, worms, sugar, uric acid). That pairing method is the aid; the pairs above are standard teaching.

## How the exam asks about it
- Match the herb to its use, usually ampalaya, lagundi, akapulko, sambong, niyog-niyogan.
- Trap: herb safety (some parts, doses or preparations are harmful) and not substituting for treatment.

## Related topics
[[Treatment of CD, NCD and Emergency Services]], [[Elements of Primary Health Care]], [[DOH]]

## Check against your textbook
- The official list of herbs, plant parts used, preparation methods and amounts; none of the doses is stated here (verify local policy).

title: Nutrition
body:
## What it is
Nutrition is a PHC element because malnutrition (too little, too much, or the wrong nutrients) raises the risk of infection, poor growth and death in children. Programs combine growth monitoring, supplementation, food fortification and feeding support.

## Must-know facts
Malnutrition recognition:
- Protein-energy malnutrition shows in the child's weight, height, and arm measurements compared with standards. Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is a quick screening tool.
- Marasmus: severe lack of overall energy intake. Very thin, wasted, "old man" face, hungry, no edema.
- Kwashiorkor: lack of protein with relatively more starch. Edema (often feet and face), swollen belly, thin or discolored hair, skin changes, apathy and irritability.
- Bilateral pitting edema in a child signals severe acute malnutrition, which is an urgent referral.
- Overnutrition and obesity also count as malnutrition.

Micronutrients (concepts):
- Vitamin A: needed for vision and immunity. Deficiency causes night blindness and, in severe cases, corneal damage. Children are given supplementation at set ages through a program; verify schedule and doses.
- Iron: deficiency causes anemia; pregnant women and young children are at risk.
- Iodine: deficiency causes goiter and developmental problems; iodized salt is a main protection.
- Zinc is used with ORS for diarrhea in many programs (verify local policy).

Food fortification:
- Fortification means adding nutrients to commonly eaten foods. Philippine law requires fortification of some staples (commonly cited items: rice, flour, cooking oil, sugar), and a separate salt iodization law exists. Fortified products may carry a program seal. Verify the exact list and law numbers.

Programs: growth monitoring (periodic weighing), supplementary feeding, nutrition education, breastfeeding promotion and complementary feeding.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Check for danger signs in the malnourished child first (poor appetite, dehydration, serious infection, severe edema): refer if present.
2. Measure weight, length/height and MUAC; plot and classify.
3. Give supplements per program schedule; feed and teach per classification.
4. Counsel on breastfeeding, complementary foods and food groups using locally affordable foods.
5. Follow up growth and household food security.

## Community and family teaching
Start complementary foods at the recommended age, give varied and fortified foods, use iodized salt, keep food clean, and bring the child for regular weighing.

## How the exam asks about it
- Differentiate marasmus vs kwashiorkor from the described child.
- Which micronutrient problem matches the sign described.
- Trap: both conditions need nutrition rehabilitation under supervision; rapid refeeding is risky.

## Memory aid
Kwashiorkor = edema ("swollen"); marasmus = "wasted". My own simplification.

## Related topics
[[Maternal and Child Health]], [[Health Promotion]], [[Elements of Primary Health Care]], [[Community Mental Health Program]]

## Check against your textbook
- Vitamin A, iron and zinc schedules and doses (none stated here), exact fortification list, law numbers and program names (verify local policy).

title: Treatment of CD, NCD and Emergency Services
body:
## What it is
This PHC element covers basic care of common communicable diseases (CD), noncommunicable diseases (NCD) and injuries/emergencies at the community level, with referral when needed.

## Must-know facts
Communicable disease treatment:
- Follow national protocols (for example for diarrhea, pneumonia, tuberculosis, malaria). Common principles: treat dehydration with oral rehydration, give antibiotics only when indicated, complete the course, and teach prevention.
- Diarrhea: assess hydration, give ORS and continue feeding; refer for severe dehydration or blood in stool.

Noncommunicable diseases:
- Major NCDs: cardiovascular disease (including hypertension), diabetes, cancer and chronic lung disease.
- Shared risk factors: tobacco, harmful alcohol use, unhealthy diet, physical inactivity.
- Community roles: screening (blood pressure, blood sugar, risk assessment), lifestyle counseling, regular medication, early referral and follow-up. A package of essential NCD interventions for primary care exists internationally; the local name and content: verify.
- Warning signs needing urgent care: severe chest pain, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, very high blood pressure with symptoms, very high or very low blood sugar with confusion.

Emergency services in the community:
- First aid and basic life support, bleeding control, splinting, wound care, burn cooling, choking relief, and safe transport.
- A functioning referral system: call ahead, send a referral note, transfer in a stable state with an escort when possible.
- Emergency hotline and ambulance availability vary: verify local numbers and policy.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Primary survey: airway, breathing, circulation, then disability/exposure. Life threats first.
2. Control bleeding and protect the neck when injury suspected.
3. Call for help or arrange transport early; do not wait for the full assessment to refer an unstable client.
4. Give first aid within scope and standing orders.
5. Document and communicate to the receiving facility.
6. Teach family prevention and follow-up.

## Key terms and steps
- Triage: sorting by urgency so the sickest get care first.
- Referral: sending to a higher level; two-way (also referring back for follow-up).

## Community and family teaching
Know danger signs, keep emergency contacts visible, take medicine as prescribed, do not use unproven remedies in emergencies, learn basic first aid and CPR.

## How the exam asks about it
- Priority questions: ABC beats everything; unstable before stable.
- Which NCD risk factor is modifiable? Smoking, diet, activity.
- Trap: choosing a long assessment or teaching before addressing an obvious emergency.

## Related topics
[[Essential Drugs]], [[Elements of Primary Health Care]], [[Nutrition]], [[Locally Endemic Diseases]], [[Health Promotion]]

## Check against your textbook
- Exact treatment protocols, program names (NCD packages), hotline numbers and referral levels (verify local policy). No drug doses are given here.
outlineRefs: 7. Treatment of CD and NCD and Emergency Services

title: Water Supply and Toilet Facilities
body:
## What it is
Safe water and proper excreta disposal are the two strongest tools against diarrheal diseases, typhoid, hepatitis A, cholera and worm infections in the community.

## Must-know facts
Water supply facilities (the classic three-level classification used in Philippine sanitation teaching; verify local standards):
- Level I (point source): a protected well or spring serving a small number of households, without a piped network.
- Level II (communal faucet or standpost): piped water to a public tap serving a group of households.
- Level III (waterworks system): piped connection to individual households.
- Typical safe-source rules: a well should be protected from contamination, sited at a safe distance from toilets and animal pens (textbooks give a distance, commonly 25 meters; verify), with a sealed top and drainage away.
- Home water treatment: boiling (rolling boil for a set time), chlorination, filtration and storing in a clean covered container. Verify local advice for time and amounts.
- Water must be tested for bacteria if the source is suspect.

Toilet facilities:
- A sanitary toilet prevents contact with excreta, keeps flies and animals away, prevents odor and does not contaminate water.
- Types: water-sealed (flush or pour-flush) toilet, pit latrine with a cover, ventilated improved pit latrine, composting toilet where suitable.
- Placement: away from the water source and downhill from wells where possible.
- Open defecation is unsafe.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Assess the source of drinking water, how it is stored and what toilets the household uses.
2. Identify the contamination risk (shared drain, nearby toilet, open container).
3. Advise the quickest safe fix: boil or chlorinate drinking water now.
4. Promote construction and use of a sanitary toilet with the barangay and household.
5. Teach handwashing with soap after toilet use and before eating or feeding.
6. Report suspected waterborne disease clusters.

## Key terms and steps
- Potable: safe to drink.
- Rolling boil: continuous bubbling; the time is given in your textbook.
- Chlorination requires the right amount and contact time; do not state numbers from memory.

## How the exam asks about it
- Classify a described facility as Level I, II or III. Key words: well or spring = I; communal tap = II; house connection = III.
- Choose the best toilet for a family or the best first action for unsafe water.
- Trap: a flushing toilet near a shallow well can still contaminate the well.

## Memory aid
Level number = how close the water is to the house: I at a source, II at a shared tap, III inside the home. My own aid.

## Related topics
[[Waste, Food Sanitation and Sanitation Laws]], [[Locally Endemic Diseases]], [[Elements of Primary Health Care]], [[Nutrition]]

## Check against your textbook
- Household counts per level, safe distances, boiling times and chlorine amounts (verify local policy).
outlineRefs: Approved Types of Water Supply Facilities

title: Waste, Food Sanitation and Sanitation Laws
body:
## What it is
This note groups three parts of environmental health: how waste is separated and disposed of, how food is kept safe, and the main laws that govern sanitation.

## Must-know facts
Waste:
- Segregate at source: biodegradable (food scraps, leaves), non-biodegradable/residual, recyclable, and special or hazardous waste (batteries, chemicals).
- Health-care waste is separated into infectious/pathological, sharps, chemical, pharmaceutical and general waste. Sharps go into puncture-resistant containers; infectious waste goes into designated bags and containers.
- Color coding is used for bins and bags. The assignment of colors is regulated and has changed over time; I am not stating a color table from memory. Verify the current DOH health-care waste and local solid-waste color codes.
- Safe disposal methods include composting, sanitary landfill, controlled treatment (such as autoclaving) and the barangay materials recovery facility. Open burning and open dumping are discouraged.

Food sanitation:
- Food-borne illness comes from contaminated food, hands, water, pests and poor storage.
- Standard safe-food principles: keep clean, separate raw and cooked, cook thoroughly, keep food at safe temperatures, and use safe water and ingredients.
- Hot foods stay hot and cold foods cold; avoid leaving food at room temperature for long.
- Food handlers need regular health examinations/certificates and should not handle food when ill with diarrhea, skin infection or respiratory infection. Establishments need sanitary permits.
- Control flies, cockroaches and rodents with clean storage and waste management.

Laws (commonly cited in nursing reviews; verify numbers and content):
- Code on Sanitation of the Philippines (PD 856): water, food, excreta, waste, housing and other sanitation rules.
- Ecological Solid Waste Management Act (RA 9003): segregation and local solid waste plans.
- Clean Water Act (RA 9275) and Clean Air Act (RA 8749): water and air quality.
- Mandatory notifiable disease reporting law (commonly RA 11332).

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Inspect and assess hazards (open dump, fly breeding, food handling, unsafe storage).
2. Protect health first: isolate or treat sick food handlers or affected persons, then remove the hazard.
3. Teach and demonstrate segregation, handwashing and safe food preparation.
4. Work with the barangay sanitary inspector and officials for enforcement.
5. Report outbreaks and keep records.

## Key terms and steps
- Sanitary inspector: the local officer who enforces sanitation rules.
- Vector: insects and rodents that carry disease; remove food, water and shelter for them.

## How the exam asks about it
- Which bin or container is right for a given waste? Reason through category first, then check your color table.
- Which action is the first step to prevent food poisoning in a community? Prevention via handwashing, cooking and storage beats treatment.
- Link a law to its topic (food, solid waste, water).

## Related topics
[[Water Supply and Toilet Facilities]], [[Locally Endemic Diseases]], [[Elements of Primary Health Care]], [[DOH]]

## Check against your textbook
- The color code tables, the law numbers, the food holding temperatures and the health certificate rules (verify local policy).

title: Community Mental Health Program
body:
## What it is
The Mental Health Program brings basic mental health care into primary care and the community, so people can get help close to home, without stigma. The national law is commonly cited as the Mental Health Act (RA 11036, 2018; verify).

## Must-know facts
- Mental health is a part of overall health. Community care tries to prevent problems, find them early, treat and support recovery in the community instead of institutions.
- Services are integrated into primary care, with referral to specialists and hospitals for severe or complex cases.
- Rights approach: dignity, informed consent, privacy and protection against discrimination.
- Common community concerns: depression, anxiety, substance use, suicide risk, stress after disasters and violence, dementia in older adults, and mental health of adolescents.
- Warning signs of risk: talking about death or wanting to die, giving away belongings, hopelessness, withdrawal, sudden changes in behavior, substance misuse, major losses.
- Stigma and myths prevent care-seeking; education reduces them.
- Barangay and community volunteers can be trained to recognize problems and refer.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Ensure safety first: if a person is at risk of harming self or others, stay with them, remove means, and get urgent help. Safety is the first priority (Maslow safety need).
2. Build rapport and listen without judgment; ask directly about suicidal thoughts when concerned, since asking does not plant the idea.
3. Assess needs and basic functioning (sleep, eating, support).
4. Provide psychological first aid and stress reduction when a crisis or disaster has happened.
5. Refer for evaluation and treatment, arrange follow-up and involve family.
6. Teach coping skills, healthy routines and how to get help.

## Key terms and steps
- Psychological first aid: practical, supportive care that offers comfort, safety and information without forcing the person to talk.
- Primary, secondary and tertiary prevention applies: promotion and stigma reduction, early detection, then rehabilitation and relapse prevention.

## Community and family teaching
Mental illness is treatable, it is not shameful or caused by weakness, encourage taking medicines as prescribed, keep a routine, avoid alcohol and drugs, and know crisis contacts (verify local numbers).

## How the exam asks about it
- Safety first with a person expressing suicidal thoughts, then therapeutic communication, then referral.
- Therapeutic responses: open, empathic, not false reassurance.
- Trap: arguing with or minimizing feelings; promising to keep a suicide plan secret.

## Related topics
[[Primary Health Care]], [[VAWC and Violence Against Women and Children]], [[Health Promotion]], [[Nutrition]]

## Check against your textbook
- Program names, the current guideline for community mental health in primary care, and local hotline numbers (verify local policy).

title: Epidemiology and Endemic Diseases
body:
## What it is
The "Locally endemic diseases" element of PHC: understanding disease patterns in the community with data, and controlling the diseases that are regularly present. This is a hub note that points to the detailed notes.

## Must-know facts
- Epidemiology and surveillance data guide which diseases to control: see [[Epidemiology and FHSIS]].
- The diseases that are regularly present in an area, with cause, spread, signs and control: see [[Locally Endemic Diseases]].
- Numbers used to describe community health: [[Vital Statistics]] and [[Incidence, Prevalence and Population Pyramid]].

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Treat urgent cases first, then report and investigate, because early reporting stops spread.
2. Analyze local data and target the biggest or fastest-growing problem.
3. Break the chain of transmission at the weakest link (agent, host or environment).

## How the exam asks about it
Identify the disease from vector or reservoir, choose the control that breaks transmission, or compute a rate.

## Related topics
[[Epidemiology and FHSIS]], [[Locally Endemic Diseases]], [[Vital Statistics]], [[Incidence, Prevalence and Population Pyramid]], [[Three Levels of Prevention]], [[Elements of Primary Health Care]]

## Check against your textbook
- Which diseases your textbook treats as locally endemic (verify local policy).

title: Environmental Sanitation
body:
## What it is
The sanitation element of PHC: making the physical environment safe through clean water, proper excreta disposal, waste management, safe food and vector control. This is a hub note that points to the detailed notes.

## Must-know facts
- Water supply levels and toilet types: [[Water Supply and Toilet Facilities]].
- Waste segregation, food safety and the main sanitation laws: [[Waste, Food Sanitation and Sanitation Laws]].
- Poor sanitation drives diarrheal disease, typhoid, hepatitis A, worm infections and vector-borne disease, so sanitation is prevention at the primary level.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Assess household water, toilet, waste and food handling.
2. Fix the highest-risk exposure first (unsafe drinking water, open defecation).
3. Teach, demonstrate and organize the community; work with the sanitary inspector.
